All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3. The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting. To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1. The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration. It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives. Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree. To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates. Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced. While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information. Note: Within this document, italicized text represents notes. These notes represent comments that are not supported by evidence but represent the author\xe2\x80\x99s opinion. For example, they discuss concessions that have been made to make the emulation instructions practical or to indicate where inconsistent or nonexistent reporting has required gaps to be filled in with best-guess estimates of adversary behavior. References are indicated in-line with bracketed numbers [#] and listed at the end of this document. All Rights Reserved 2-2 Adversary Objectives: Reporting indicates APT3 actors are interested in exfiltration of documents [3]. They have been known to target printers and file shares [3]. They also target intellectual property, often industrial in nature. [4]. Background: APT3 is a China-based threat group. APT3 has traditionally targeted a myriad of US and international targets; however, reporting dated September 2016 indicates the group shifted focus around March 2016 to target Hong Kong organizations [3]. APT3\xe2\x80\x99s process can be broken up into three main phases as shown below: 1. Initial Setup of command and control (C2), defense evasion techniques, and getting initial compromise 2. Discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence, and execution 3. Collection, data staging, and exfiltration Figure 1 APT3's Three Phases of Action These phases are broken up into more detail in the following sections. The next section is about the tools that APT3 uses for their operations, how to emulate them, and what ATT&CK tactics and techniques they correspond to. Command-line examples, as well as descriptions of what the tools do, are included in the accompanying \xe2\x80\x9cAPT3 Adversary Emulation Field Manual\xe2\x80\x9d for reference. 2.1 APT3 Tools APT3 uses a combination of custom and openly available tools. Because custom adversary tools can have hidden functionality, be difficult to tailor to new environments, or utilize server-side controllers which may be unavailable, recommendations are made for replacements that can accurately perform similar activity. Emulation Phases APT3 disseminates spam-like phishing campaigns with various payload delivery methods [1]. Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have. Admin access is an obvious main target due to the increased access it will likely provide. The actors then drop multiple backdoors, usually 2-4 on the initial system and 5+ versions within the first few hops, with independent C2 profiles for redundancy [Redundant Access \xe2\x80\x93 T1108]. Next they then dump as many credentials as possible, and quickly continue spreading throughout the network. They specifically go after file servers and print servers [1] [3]. Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15]. In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data. The sections below show how APT3 acts through their entire lifecycle. Phase 1 documents what happens during initial compromise, phase 2 highlights techniques used during network propagation, and phase 3 documents one way they have been known to perform exfiltration. 3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment. APT3 primarily conducts initial compromise using spear phishing, delivering implants through both malicious attachments and malicious links. They have used new 0-days on multiple browsers [15]. They have targeted existing 0-days in Internet Explorer [2], Windows [2], and Flash [14]. They have also been known to compromise weakly secured legitimate websites to which users are directed through spear phishing emails [16]. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1108 Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited. All Rights Reserved 3-12 3.1.1 Implant Command and Control APT3 implants issue command and control (C2) traffic as HTTP GET requests that beacon at set intervals [14]. The HTTP Cookie field contains information for the C2 server, which responds with a webpage that contains the command encoded within a specific HTML tag [15]. APT3 implants have also been known to use custom binary protocols [2]. Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15]. Some of the Pirpi instances have been known to also use SSL for their communications and even include public/private keys within the binaries [17]. This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14]. 3.1.2 Defense Evasion Many of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s open source tools are customized or modified to prevent detection. Additionally, APT3\xe2\x80\x99s malware uses a series of anti-disassembly techniques [3], including requiring certain command line parameters to run [17]. These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment. It is recommended to use anti-antivirus (AV) capabilities to prevent AV detection of commonly available tools. If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing. An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19]. ATTACK techniques: T1027 \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information, T1045 \xe2\x80\x93 Software Packing, T1066 \xe2\x80\x93 Indicator Removal from Tools. 3.1.3 Initial Access For Initial Compromise, both web server drive-by and malicious attachments are within APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft. The Social Engineering Toolkit (free) [20] and Cobalt Strike (paid) [6] have features that support these methods. 3.1.3.1 Case 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Spear Phishing with Browser Exploit [2] In late November 2014 an APT3 campaign used a spear phishing email (see Appendix A) containing a link to a malicious site. The site contained JavaScript that triggered CVE-2014-6332 (an Internet Explorer exploit [21]) which launched a VBscript and PowerShell based payload. The PowerShell script in turn downloaded and ran a stager which dropped two files, \xe2\x80\x9cdoc.exe\xe2\x80\x9d and \xe2\x80\x9ctest.exe\xe2\x80\x9d. \xe2\x80\x9cdoc.exe\xe2\x80\x9d attempts to trigger CVE-2014-4113 (a Windows Kernel exploit [22]) and run \xe2\x80\x9ctest.exe\xe2\x80\x9d with the resultant elevated privileges. \xe2\x80\x9ctest.exe\xe2\x80\x9d runs two commands: cmd.exe /C whoami schtasks /create /tn "mysc" /tr C:\\Users\\Public\\test.exe /sc ONLOGON /ru "System" The first command is used to check that the process is running as SYSTEM. The second establishes persistence via Schtasks. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1027 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1027 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1045 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1066 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1066 Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited. This dropper supports writing to or executing files at the following locations: C:\\Users\\[Username]\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\notepad1.exe C:\\Users\\[Username]\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\notepad.exe C:\\Users\\[Username]\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\notepad2.exe C:\\Users\\[Username]\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\newnotepad.exe In addition, the software supports exfiltrating the file written at the following location [T1074 \xe2\x80\x93 Data Staged]: C:\\Users\\[Username]\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\note.txt In October 2014, a downloader like \xe2\x80\x9ctest.exe\xe2\x80\x9d was observed to download Pirpi. 3.1.3.2 Spear Phishing with Malicious RAR Attachment [3] In attacks dating late 2015 to early 2016 APT3 has been known to use a zip archive containing a Windows shortcut file with an Internet Explorer logo. Clicking on this link led to a download of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Pirpi RAT. 3.1.3.3 Spear Phishing with Malicious RAR Attachment [7] In attacks reported in June 2014, APT3 actors sent a RAR archive as an email attachment. It contained a resume and program purported to be written by the job candidate. The program, ttcalc.exe, contained a legitimate version of TTCalc but also dropped Pirpi to: %USERPROFILE%/Application Data/mt.dat And a bat file that was saved at [T1064 \xe2\x80\x93 Scripting]: %USERPROFILE%/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/vc.bat The bat file contained the following script: @echo off cmd.exe /C start rundll32.exe "C:\\Documents and Settings\\admin\\Application Data\\mt.dat" UpdvaMt The bat file will be triggered when the user logged in and would have caused Pirpi to start with rundll32 [T1085 \xe2\x80\x93 Rundll32]. 3.1.3.4 Spear Phishing with Malicious RAR Attachment [7] Reported in June 2014, APT3 actors sent an encrypted self-extracting RAR attachment. The RAR contained a trojanized setup program which attempts to drop and run ttcalcBAK.exe another self-extracting RAR which drops a DLL version of the PlugX RAT at: %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\\chrome_frame_helper https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1074 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1074 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1064 https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/T1085 Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited. In both cases the Flash exploit loaded the payload (the Pirpi RAT) from specially crafted GIF images. 3.1.3.6 Victim Profiling [16] Reported in July 2015, APT3 used spear phising to direct targets to a compromised site. This site had ScanBox installed which was used to profile the victims and in some cases, deliver exploits to selected victims. 3.2 Phase 2 - Network Propagation The goal of the Network Propagation phase is to identify and move to desired systems within the target environment with the intention of discovering credentials and documents for exfiltration. Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent. One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs. Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use. There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation. Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft. Where necessary we fill in details with best guesses or recommendations. The process within this phase can be described with the below diagram. Each step within this phase is broken out by ATT&CK tactic and the corresponding APT3 specific techniques documented in reports. Based on the commands available in APT3\xe2\x80\x99s toolset, there is a lot of time spent enumerating domain groups with elevated permissions like \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, \xe2\x80\x9cEnterprise Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, and \xe2\x80\x9cPower Users\xe2\x80\x9d [T1069 - Permission Groups Discovery]. When doing discovery, certain actions are very closely intertwined (as shown grouped together in the above diagram). Querying the domain for the \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d group [T1069 \xe2\x80\x93 Permission Groups Discovery] returns the users that are members of that group, which then involves looking up those users to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re part of any other interesting groups [T1087 \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery]. This process can repeat for a while as all interesting users and groups are enumerated. Similarly, querying systems for their configuration [T1016 \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Configuration Discovery] and their current network connections [T1049 \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Connections Discovery] are heavily integrated. 3.2.1.2 Local Privilege Escalation Credential dumping and persistence may require local privilege escalation if the attacker does not have control of a high integrity process; however, the only reporting available on local privilege escalation methods used by APT3 is CVE-2014-4113 [2]. It is possible that their strong reliance on credential access (detailed later) allows them to use credentials with increasing levels of access in place of other local privilege escalation mechanisms. Their perceived focus during this phase, however, is on finding credentials that allow direct admin permissions. In this case, control falls through to credential access or persistence. During an engagement, adversary emulators may find it necessary to perform local privilege escalation due to time constraints. Most common frameworks (including Metasploit and Cobalt Strike) contain some methods for privilege escalation. Also, UACBypass [24] and PowerUp [9] are common and freely available tools that may be used to perform Privilege Escalation. APT3 has replaced the Sticky Keys binary (C:\\Windows\\System32\\sethc.exe) with cmd.exe [T1015 - Accessibility Features] and enabled Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) if it is not already enabled [T1076 \xe2\x80\x93 Remote Desktop Protocol]. This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23]. APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [T1136 \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account]. Presumably this is done for easier future access. Recommendation: On new hosts, establish persistence by creating a service or schtasks. On systems where RDP capabilities are desired, it might also be useful to enable sticky keys and RDP. 3.2.1.4 Credential Access APT3 uses many forms of credential access. They used customized versions of pwdump, and later a custom compiled version of mimikatz, to search for cached Windows credentials [T1003 - Credential Dumping] as well as ChromePass and Lazagne [(T1081 - Credentials in Files], to search though browser and other credential caches. Their pwdump tool injects itself into lsass.exe and is executed by running the GetHash export of the lsremora.dll [3] Mimikatz is used to dump plaintext credentials by injecting into lsass.exe. [T1003 - Credential Dumping]. They also install a keylogger, which can be used to discover credentials and remote systems [T1056 - Input Capture]. This keylogger installs itself as a service and records keystrokes in encrypted files such as thumbcache_96.dbx [T1027 \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information] [3]. This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information. Pirpi has commands that list servers in the domain, list TCP connections and retrieve connected users (T1049 - Network Connections Discovery), and list Domain Controllers (T1018 - Remote System Discovery). Some of this information may be used to identify target hosts for lateral movement. In addition to built-in Windows utilities, there are some open source tools which collect similar information. APT3 will quickly spread to other machines as fast as possible, often checking for easy password reuse by trying to mount shares from other machines via \xe2\x80\x9cnet use\xe2\x80\x9d [T1078 \xe2\x80\x93 Valid Accounts] [T1077 - Windows Admin Shares] [T1110 \xe2\x80\x93 Brute Force]. APT3 prioritizes file and printer servers. Remote Copy and Execution APT3 uses a custom tool called RemoteCMD that can run commands on a remote system. It\xe2\x80\x99s not clear what protocol(s) are being used, but RemoteCMD supports file operations (upload, download, delete and rename) service operations (creation, deletion, start and stop) and scheduled tasks (AT,schtasks). Presumably these are done over SMB (files), Remote Service (services) and Remote Schtasks (AT). All Rights Reserved 3-19 3.3 Phase 3 - Exfiltration It\xe2\x80\x99s likely that APT3 will compromise a network to a certain degree of satisfaction before starting to exfil, due to stealth concerns. Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools. The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012. For exfiltration, they will identify Office documents on the computer [23] [T1005 - Data from Local System]. They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [T1002 - Data Compressed]. This archive will then be stored in the recycle bin [23], usually on a machine designated as a staging server, which they move the exfiltration through [T1074 - Data Staged]. Data is exfiltrated over port 443 which is typically HTTPS traffic, however they have used SSL encryption [17] and normal HTTP [23] [T1043 - Commonly Used Port] . All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3.
The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1.
The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information.
Note: Within this document, italicized text represents notes.
These notes represent comments that are not supported by evidence but represent the author\xe2\x80\x99s opinion.

For example, they discuss concessions that have been made to make the emulation instructions practical or to indicate where inconsistent or nonexistent reporting has required gaps to be filled in with best-guess estimates of adversary behavior.
References are indicated in-line with bracketed numbers [#] and listed at the end of this document.

Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have.
Admin access is an obvious main target due to the increased access it will likely provide.
The actors then drop multiple backdoors, usually 2-4 on the initial system and 5+ versions within the first few hops, with independent C2 profiles for redundancy [Redundant Access \xe2\x80\x93 ].
Next they then dump as many credentials as possible, and quickly continue spreading throughout the network.
They specifically go after file servers and print servers [1] [3].

Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15].
In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data.
The sections below show how APT3 acts through their entire lifecycle.
Phase 1 documents what happens during initial compromise, phase 2 highlights techniques used during network propagation, and phase 3 documents one way they have been known to perform exfiltration.
3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment.

All Rights Reserved 3-12 3.1.1 Implant Command and Control APT3 implants issue command and control (C2) traffic as HTTP GET requests that beacon at set intervals [14].
The HTTP Cookie field contains information for the C2 server, which responds with a webpage that contains the command encoded within a specific HTML tag [15].
APT3 implants have also been known to use custom binary protocols [2].
Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15].
Some of the Pirpi instances have been known to also use SSL for their communications and even include public/private keys within the binaries [17].
This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14].
3.1.2 Defense Evasion Many of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s open source tools are customized or modified to prevent detection.
Additionally, APT3\xe2\x80\x99s malware uses a series of anti-disassembly techniques [3], including requiring certain command line parameters to run [17].
These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment.
It is recommended to use anti-antivirus (AV) capabilities to prevent AV detection of commonly available tools.
If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing.
An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19].
ATTACK techniques: \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information, \xe2\x80\x93 Software Packing, \xe2\x80\x93 Indicator Removal from Tools.

3.2 Phase 2 - Network Propagation The goal of the Network Propagation phase is to identify and move to desired systems within the target environment with the intention of discovering credentials and documents for exfiltration.
Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent.
One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs.
Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use.
There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation.
Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
Where necessary we fill in details with best guesses or recommendations.

All Rights Reserved 3-17 3.2.1.3 Persistence APT3 has used multiple methods for persistence: creating a service [23] ( - New Service), creating a scheduled task [2] ( - Scheduled Task), and also by placing scripts in the Startup Folder [7] [ - Registry Run Keys/Start Folder].
This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23].
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account].

They used customized versions of pwdump, and later a custom compiled version of mimikatz, to search for cached Windows credentials [ - Credential Dumping] as well as ChromePass and Lazagne [( - Credentials in Files], to search though browser and other credential caches.

Their pwdump tool injects itself into lsass.exe and is executed by running the GetHash export of the lsremora.dll [3] Mimikatz is used to dump plaintext credentials by injecting into lsass.exe. [ - Credential Dumping].
They also install a keylogger, which can be used to discover credentials and remote systems [ - Input Capture].
This keylogger installs itself as a service and records keystrokes in encrypted files such as thumbcache_96.dbx [ \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information] [3].

This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information.
In addition to built-in Windows utilities, there are some open source tools which collect similar information.
APT3 prioritizes file and printer servers.
Remote Copy and Execution APT3 uses a custom tool called RemoteCMD that can run commands on a remote system.

It\xe2\x80\x99s not clear what protocol(s) are being used, but RemoteCMD supports file operations (upload, download, delete and rename) service operations (creation, deletion, start and stop) and scheduled tasks (AT,schtasks).
Presumably these are done over SMB (files), Remote Service (services) and Remote Schtasks (AT).

All Rights Reserved 3-19 3.3 Phase 3 - Exfiltration It\xe2\x80\x99s likely that APT3 will compromise a network to a certain degree of satisfaction before starting to exfil, due to stealth concerns.
Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools.
The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012.
For exfiltration, they will identify Office documents on the computer [23] [ - Data from Local System].
They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].
This archive will then be stored in the recycle bin [23], usually on a machine designated as a staging server, which they move the exfiltration through [ - Data Staged].
Data is exfiltrated over port 443 which is typically HTTPS traffic, however they have used SSL encryption [17] and normal HTTP [23] [ - Commonly Used Port] .

The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1.
The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information.

Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have.
Admin access is an obvious main target due to the increased access it will likely provide.
The actors then drop multiple backdoors, usually 2-4 on the initial system and 5+ versions within the first few hops, with independent C2 profiles for redundancy [Redundant Access \xe2\x80\x93 ].
They specifically go after file servers and print servers [1] [3].

Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15].
In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data.
Phase 1 documents what happens during initial compromise, phase 2 highlights techniques used during network propagation, and phase 3 documents one way they have been known to perform exfiltration.
3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment.
APT3 primarily conducts initial compromise using spear phishing, delivering implants through both malicious attachments and malicious links.

They have also been known to compromise weakly secured legitimate websites to which users are directed through spear phishing emails [16]. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.

All Rights Reserved 3-12 3.1.1 Implant Command and Control APT3 implants issue command and control (C2) traffic as HTTP GET requests that beacon at set intervals [14].
The HTTP Cookie field contains information for the C2 server, which responds with a webpage that contains the command encoded within a specific HTML tag [15].
APT3 implants have also been known to use custom binary protocols [2].
Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15].
Some of the Pirpi instances have been known to also use SSL for their communications and even include public/private keys within the binaries [17].
This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14].
3.1.2 Defense Evasion Many of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s open source tools are customized or modified to prevent detection.
Additionally, APT3\xe2\x80\x99s malware uses a series of anti-disassembly techniques [3], including requiring certain command line parameters to run [17].
These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment.
If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing.
An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19].
ATTACK techniques: \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information, \xe2\x80\x93 Software Packing, \xe2\x80\x93 Indicator Removal from Tools.
3.1.3 Initial Access For Initial Compromise, both web server drive-by and malicious attachments are within APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
The Social Engineering Toolkit (free) [20] and Cobalt Strike (paid) [6] have features that support these methods.
3.1.3.1 Case 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Spear Phishing with Browser Exploit [2] In late November 2014 an APT3 campaign used a spear phishing email (see Appendix A) containing a link to a malicious site.
The site contained JavaScript that triggered CVE-2014-6332 (an Internet Explorer exploit [21]) which launched a VBscript and PowerShell based payload.

3.1.3.5 Flash Exploit with Malware Concealed Within GIF [14] Reported in 2015, two different APT3 campaigns targeted Flash exploits, CVE-2014-1776 and CVE-2015-3113.
In both cases the Flash exploit loaded the payload (the Pirpi RAT) from specially crafted GIF images.
3.1.3.6 Victim Profiling [16] Reported in July 2015, APT3 used spear phising to direct targets to a compromised site.
This site had ScanBox installed which was used to profile the victims and in some cases, deliver exploits to selected victims.
Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent.
One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs.
Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use.
There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation.
Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
Where necessary we fill in details with best guesses or recommendations.

Based on the commands available in APT3\xe2\x80\x99s toolset, there is a lot of time spent enumerating domain groups with elevated permissions like \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, \xe2\x80\x9cEnterprise Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, and \xe2\x80\x9cPower Users\xe2\x80\x9d [ - Permission Groups Discovery].

When doing discovery, certain actions are very closely intertwined (as shown grouped together in the above diagram).

Querying the domain for the \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d group [ \xe2\x80\x93 Permission Groups Discovery] returns the users that are members of that group, which then involves looking up those users to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re part of any other interesting groups [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].
This process can repeat for a while as all interesting users and groups are enumerated.

Similarly, querying systems for their configuration [ \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Configuration Discovery] and their current network connections [ \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Connections Discovery] are heavily integrated.
Also, UACBypass [24] and PowerUp [9] are common and freely available tools that may be used to perform Privilege Escalation.

APT3 has replaced the Sticky Keys binary (C:\\Windows\\System32\\sethc.exe) with cmd.exe [ - Accessibility Features] and enabled Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) if it is not already enabled [ \xe2\x80\x93 Remote Desktop Protocol].
This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23].
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account].

This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information.
Pirpi has commands that list servers in the domain, list TCP connections and retrieve connected users ( - Network Connections Discovery), and list Domain Controllers ( - Remote System Discovery).
In addition to built-in Windows utilities, there are some open source tools which collect similar information.
Remote Copy and Execution APT3 uses a custom tool called RemoteCMD that can run commands on a remote system.

It\xe2\x80\x99s not clear what protocol(s) are being used, but RemoteCMD supports file operations (upload, download, delete and rename) service operations (creation, deletion, start and stop) and scheduled tasks (AT,schtasks).

Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools.
The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012.
They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].
This archive will then be stored in the recycle bin [23], usually on a machine designated as a staging server, which they move the exfiltration through [ - Data Staged].
Data is exfiltrated over port 443 which is typically HTTPS traffic, however they have used SSL encryption [17] and normal HTTP [23] [ - Commonly Used Port] .

All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3.
The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1.
The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information.
Note: Within this document, italicized text represents notes.
These notes represent comments that are not supported by evidence but represent the author\xe2\x80\x99s opinion.

For example, they discuss concessions that have been made to make the emulation instructions practical or to indicate where inconsistent or nonexistent reporting has required gaps to be filled in with best-guess estimates of adversary behavior.
References are indicated in-line with bracketed numbers [#] and listed at the end of this document.

All Rights Reserved 2-2 Adversary Objectives: Reporting indicates APT3 actors are interested in exfiltration of documents [3].
They also target intellectual property, often industrial in nature. [4].
Background: APT3 is a China-based threat group.

APT3 has traditionally targeted a myriad of US and international targets; however, reporting dated September 2016 indicates the group shifted focus around March 2016 to target Hong Kong organizations [3].
APT3\xe2\x80\x99s process can be broken up into three main phases as shown below: 1.
Initial Setup of command and control (C2), defense evasion techniques, and getting initial compromise 2.
Collection, data staging, and exfiltration Figure 1 APT3's Three Phases of Action These phases are broken up into more detail in the following sections.
The next section is about the tools that APT3 uses for their operations, how to emulate them, and what ATT&CK tactics and techniques they correspond to.
Command-line examples, as well as descriptions of what the tools do, are included in the accompanying \xe2\x80\x9cAPT3 Adversary Emulation Field Manual\xe2\x80\x9d for reference.
2.1 APT3 Tools APT3 uses a combination of custom and openly available tools.

Because custom adversary tools can have hidden functionality, be difficult to tailor to new environments, or utilize server-side controllers which may be unavailable, recommendations are made for replacements that can accurately perform similar activity.

Emulation Phases APT3 disseminates spam-like phishing campaigns with various payload delivery methods [1].
Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have.
Admin access is an obvious main target due to the increased access it will likely provide.
The actors then drop multiple backdoors, usually 2-4 on the initial system and 5+ versions within the first few hops, with independent C2 profiles for redundancy [Redundant Access \xe2\x80\x93 ].
Next they then dump as many credentials as possible, and quickly continue spreading throughout the network.
They specifically go after file servers and print servers [1] [3].

Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15].
In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data.
The sections below show how APT3 acts through their entire lifecycle.
Phase 1 documents what happens during initial compromise, phase 2 highlights techniques used during network propagation, and phase 3 documents one way they have been known to perform exfiltration.
3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment.
APT3 primarily conducts initial compromise using spear phishing, delivering implants through both malicious attachments and malicious links.
They have used new 0-days on multiple browsers [15].
They have targeted existing 0-days in Internet Explorer [2], Windows [2], and Flash [14].

They have also been known to compromise weakly secured legitimate websites to which users are directed through spear phishing emails [16]. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.

All Rights Reserved 3-12 3.1.1 Implant Command and Control APT3 implants issue command and control (C2) traffic as HTTP GET requests that beacon at set intervals [14].
The HTTP Cookie field contains information for the C2 server, which responds with a webpage that contains the command encoded within a specific HTML tag [15].
Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15].
Some of the Pirpi instances have been known to also use SSL for their communications and even include public/private keys within the binaries [17].
This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14].
3.1.2 Defense Evasion Many of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s open source tools are customized or modified to prevent detection.
Additionally, APT3\xe2\x80\x99s malware uses a series of anti-disassembly techniques [3], including requiring certain command line parameters to run [17].
These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment.
It is recommended to use anti-antivirus (AV) capabilities to prevent AV detection of commonly available tools.
If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing.
An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19].
ATTACK techniques: \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information, \xe2\x80\x93 Software Packing, \xe2\x80\x93 Indicator Removal from Tools.
3.1.3 Initial Access For Initial Compromise, both web server drive-by and malicious attachments are within APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
The Social Engineering Toolkit (free) [20] and Cobalt Strike (paid) [6] have features that support these methods.
3.1.3.1 Case 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Spear Phishing with Browser Exploit [2] In late November 2014 an APT3 campaign used a spear phishing email (see Appendix A) containing a link to a malicious site.
The site contained JavaScript that triggered CVE-2014-6332 (an Internet Explorer exploit [21]) which launched a VBscript and PowerShell based payload.

3.1.3.2 Spear Phishing with Malicious RAR Attachment [3] In attacks dating late 2015 to early 2016 APT3 has been known to use a zip archive containing a Windows shortcut file with an Internet Explorer logo.
Clicking on this link led to a download of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Pirpi RAT.
3.1.3.3 Spear Phishing with Malicious RAR Attachment [7] In attacks reported in June 2014, APT3 actors sent a RAR archive as an email attachment.
It contained a resume and program purported to be written by the job candidate.

3.1.3.5 Flash Exploit with Malware Concealed Within GIF [14] Reported in 2015, two different APT3 campaigns targeted Flash exploits, CVE-2014-1776 and CVE-2015-3113.
In both cases the Flash exploit loaded the payload (the Pirpi RAT) from specially crafted GIF images.
3.1.3.6 Victim Profiling [16] Reported in July 2015, APT3 used spear phising to direct targets to a compromised site.
This site had ScanBox installed which was used to profile the victims and in some cases, deliver exploits to selected victims.

3.2 Phase 2 - Network Propagation The goal of the Network Propagation phase is to identify and move to desired systems within the target environment with the intention of discovering credentials and documents for exfiltration.
Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent.
One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs.
Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use.
There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation.
Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
Where necessary we fill in details with best guesses or recommendations.

Each step within this phase is broken out by ATT&CK tactic and the corresponding APT3 specific techniques documented in reports.

Based on the commands available in APT3\xe2\x80\x99s toolset, there is a lot of time spent enumerating domain groups with elevated permissions like \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, \xe2\x80\x9cEnterprise Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, and \xe2\x80\x9cPower Users\xe2\x80\x9d [ - Permission Groups Discovery].

When doing discovery, certain actions are very closely intertwined (as shown grouped together in the above diagram).

Querying the domain for the \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d group [ \xe2\x80\x93 Permission Groups Discovery] returns the users that are members of that group, which then involves looking up those users to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re part of any other interesting groups [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].
This process can repeat for a while as all interesting users and groups are enumerated.

3.2.1.2 Local Privilege Escalation Credential dumping and persistence may require local privilege escalation if the attacker does not have control of a high integrity process; however, the only reporting available on local privilege escalation methods used by APT3 is CVE-2014-4113 [2].

It is possible that their strong reliance on credential access (detailed later) allows them to use credentials with increasing levels of access in place of other local privilege escalation mechanisms.
Their perceived focus during this phase, however, is on finding credentials that allow direct admin permissions.
In this case, control falls through to credential access or persistence.
During an engagement, adversary emulators may find it necessary to perform local privilege escalation due to time constraints.
Most common frameworks (including Metasploit and Cobalt Strike) contain some methods for privilege escalation.
Also, UACBypass [24] and PowerUp [9] are common and freely available tools that may be used to perform Privilege Escalation.

APT3 has replaced the Sticky Keys binary (C:\\Windows\\System32\\sethc.exe) with cmd.exe [ - Accessibility Features] and enabled Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) if it is not already enabled [ \xe2\x80\x93 Remote Desktop Protocol].
This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23].
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account].
Recommendation: On new hosts, establish persistence by creating a service or schtasks.
On systems where RDP capabilities are desired, it might also be useful to enable sticky keys and RDP.
3.2.1.4 Credential Access APT3 uses many forms of credential access.

Their pwdump tool injects itself into lsass.exe and is executed by running the GetHash export of the lsremora.dll [3] Mimikatz is used to dump plaintext credentials by injecting into lsass.exe. [ - Credential Dumping].

This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information.
In addition to built-in Windows utilities, there are some open source tools which collect similar information.

APT3 will quickly spread to other machines as fast as possible, often checking for easy password reuse by trying to mount shares from other machines via \xe2\x80\x9cnet use\xe2\x80\x9d [ \xe2\x80\x93 Valid Accounts] [ - Windows Admin Shares] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Brute Force].
Remote Copy and Execution APT3 uses a custom tool called RemoteCMD that can run commands on a remote system.

It\xe2\x80\x99s not clear what protocol(s) are being used, but RemoteCMD supports file operations (upload, download, delete and rename) service operations (creation, deletion, start and stop) and scheduled tasks (AT,schtasks).

All Rights Reserved 3-19 3.3 Phase 3 - Exfiltration It\xe2\x80\x99s likely that APT3 will compromise a network to a certain degree of satisfaction before starting to exfil, due to stealth concerns.
Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools.
The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012.
For exfiltration, they will identify Office documents on the computer [23] [ - Data from Local System].
They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].
Data is exfiltrated over port 443 which is typically HTTPS traffic, however they have used SSL encryption [17] and normal HTTP [23] [ - Commonly Used Port] .

The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information.

APT3 implants have also been known to use custom binary protocols [2].
Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15].

All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3.
The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

For example, they discuss concessions that have been made to make the emulation instructions practical or to indicate where inconsistent or nonexistent reporting has required gaps to be filled in with best-guess estimates of adversary behavior.

APT3 Overview ATT&CK Group ID: Group/G0022 Aliases: APT3, Gothic Panda, Pirpi, UPS Team, Buckeye, Threat Group-0110, TG-0110 Operations: Clandestine Wolf, Clandestine Fox [1], Operation Double Tap [2] Target Industries: Aerospace and Defense, Construction and Engineering, High Tech, Telecommunications, Transportation [1] 1 https://attack.mitre.org https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Group/G0022 Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.
All Rights Reserved 2-2 Adversary Objectives: Reporting indicates APT3 actors are interested in exfiltration of documents [3].
Background: APT3 is a China-based threat group.
APT3\xe2\x80\x99s process can be broken up into three main phases as shown below: 1.
Initial Setup of command and control (C2), defense evasion techniques, and getting initial compromise 2.
Discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence, and execution 3.
Collection, data staging, and exfiltration Figure 1 APT3's Three Phases of Action These phases are broken up into more detail in the following sections.
The next section is about the tools that APT3 uses for their operations, how to emulate them, and what ATT&CK tactics and techniques they correspond to.
Command-line examples, as well as descriptions of what the tools do, are included in the accompanying \xe2\x80\x9cAPT3 Adversary Emulation Field Manual\xe2\x80\x9d for reference.
2.1 APT3 Tools APT3 uses a combination of custom and openly available tools.

Because custom adversary tools can have hidden functionality, be difficult to tailor to new environments, or utilize server-side controllers which may be unavailable, recommendations are made for replacements that can accurately perform similar activity.

All Rights Reserved 2-3 replacement tools will typically leave different footprints than adversary tools, specifically different file hashes, command line arguments, Antivirus detection, API calls, and network signatures.
The following table describes how to emulate the tools as well as detailing which ATT&CK Tactics are represented by them.

This section aims to break down these custom tools from the table above a bit further into their specific functions and show how they relate to ATT&CK, Windows utilities, and toolkits that are open source and commercially available.

Modules within PlugX leverage other PlugX modules to perform functions, for example, the Disk module allows other modules to use any of the functions it provides on the disk, such as execute, create new files, copy, delete, etc..

Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have.
Admin access is an obvious main target due to the increased access it will likely provide.
The actors then drop multiple backdoors, usually 2-4 on the initial system and 5+ versions within the first few hops, with independent C2 profiles for redundancy [Redundant Access \xe2\x80\x93 ].
Next they then dump as many credentials as possible, and quickly continue spreading throughout the network.

Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15].
In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data.
Phase 1 documents what happens during initial compromise, phase 2 highlights techniques used during network propagation, and phase 3 documents one way they have been known to perform exfiltration.
3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment.
APT3 implants have also been known to use custom binary protocols [2].
Pirpi.2014 and Pirpi.2015 both contain several kinds of sleep and anti-sandbox strategies that cause the RAT to pause between executions [15].
This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14].
These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment.
If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing.
An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19].
3.1.3 Initial Access For Initial Compromise, both web server drive-by and malicious attachments are within APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
The Social Engineering Toolkit (free) [20] and Cobalt Strike (paid) [6] have features that support these methods.

3.2 Phase 2 - Network Propagation The goal of the Network Propagation phase is to identify and move to desired systems within the target environment with the intention of discovering credentials and documents for exfiltration.
Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent.
One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs.
Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use.
There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation.
Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
Each step within this phase is broken out by ATT&CK tactic and the corresponding APT3 specific techniques documented in reports.

A command-line reference for emulating the specific ATT&CK techniques with built-in Windows utilities, Cobalt Strike, and Metasploit can be found in the accompanying \xe2\x80\x9cAPT3 Adversary Emulation Field Manual\xe2\x80\x9d. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.

Based on the commands available in APT3\xe2\x80\x99s toolset, there is a lot of time spent enumerating domain groups with elevated permissions like \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, \xe2\x80\x9cEnterprise Admins\xe2\x80\x9d, and \xe2\x80\x9cPower Users\xe2\x80\x9d [ - Permission Groups Discovery].
There\xe2\x80\x99s also Figure 2 APT3 Phase 2 Flow Chart https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.
All Rights Reserved 3-16 a heavy emphasis on enumerating users in these special groups with the \xe2\x80\x9cnet user\xe2\x80\x9d command [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].

Querying the domain for the \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d group [ \xe2\x80\x93 Permission Groups Discovery] returns the users that are members of that group, which then involves looking up those users to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re part of any other interesting groups [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].

Similarly, querying systems for their configuration [ \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Configuration Discovery] and their current network connections [ \xe2\x80\x93 System Network Connections Discovery] are heavily integrated.

It is possible that their strong reliance on credential access (detailed later) allows them to use credentials with increasing levels of access in place of other local privilege escalation mechanisms.
Their perceived focus during this phase, however, is on finding credentials that allow direct admin permissions.
In this case, control falls through to credential access or persistence.
During an engagement, adversary emulators may find it necessary to perform local privilege escalation due to time constraints.
Also, UACBypass [24] and PowerUp [9] are common and freely available tools that may be used to perform Privilege Escalation.

All Rights Reserved 3-17 3.2.1.3 Persistence APT3 has used multiple methods for persistence: creating a service [23] ( - New Service), creating a scheduled task [2] ( - Scheduled Task), and also by placing scripts in the Startup Folder [7] [ - Registry Run Keys/Start Folder].

APT3 has replaced the Sticky Keys binary (C:\\Windows\\System32\\sethc.exe) with cmd.exe [ - Accessibility Features] and enabled Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) if it is not already enabled [ \xe2\x80\x93 Remote Desktop Protocol].
This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23].
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account].
Presumably this is done for easier future access.
Recommendation: On new hosts, establish persistence by creating a service or schtasks.
On systems where RDP capabilities are desired, it might also be useful to enable sticky keys and RDP.
3.2.1.4 Credential Access APT3 uses many forms of credential access.
They also install a keylogger, which can be used to discover credentials and remote systems [ - Input Capture].

All Rights Reserved 3-18 3.2.2 Lateral Movement Though publicly reported information on how APT3 enumerates machines aside from related commands in APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tools, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to use \xe2\x80\x9cnet view\xe2\x80\x9d and dsquery to do so.
This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information.
Pirpi has commands that list servers in the domain, list TCP connections and retrieve connected users ( - Network Connections Discovery), and list Domain Controllers ( - Remote System Discovery).

APT3 will quickly spread to other machines as fast as possible, often checking for easy password reuse by trying to mount shares from other machines via \xe2\x80\x9cnet use\xe2\x80\x9d [ \xe2\x80\x93 Valid Accounts] [ - Windows Admin Shares] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Brute Force].
Remote Copy and Execution APT3 uses a custom tool called RemoteCMD that can run commands on a remote system.

It\xe2\x80\x99s not clear what protocol(s) are being used, but RemoteCMD supports file operations (upload, download, delete and rename) service operations (creation, deletion, start and stop) and scheduled tasks (AT,schtasks).
Presumably these are done over SMB (files), Remote Service (services) and Remote Schtasks (AT).

All Rights Reserved 3-19 3.3 Phase 3 - Exfiltration It\xe2\x80\x99s likely that APT3 will compromise a network to a certain degree of satisfaction before starting to exfil, due to stealth concerns.
Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools.
The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012.
They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].
This archive will then be stored in the recycle bin [23], usually on a machine designated as a staging server, which they move the exfiltration through [ - Data Staged].

All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3.
The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1.
It discusses tools, methods, style, tradecraft, and end state objectives.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

APT3 has replaced the Sticky Keys binary (C:\\Windows\\System32\\sethc.exe) with cmd.exe [ - Accessibility Features] and enabled Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) if it is not already enabled [ \xe2\x80\x93 Remote Desktop Protocol].
This specific Persistence technique has an added benefit of allowing an operator to open a command prompt when connected over RDP without having to provide valid credentials [23].
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, for example \xe2\x80\x9csupport_388945a0\xe2\x80\x9d, and add them to the local admin group [23] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Create Account].
3.2.1.4 Credential Access APT3 uses many forms of credential access.

They used customized versions of pwdump, and later a custom compiled version of mimikatz, to search for cached Windows credentials [ - Credential Dumping] as well as ChromePass and Lazagne [( - Credentials in Files], to search though browser and other credential caches.

Their pwdump tool injects itself into lsass.exe and is executed by running the GetHash export of the lsremora.dll [3] Mimikatz is used to dump plaintext credentials by injecting into lsass.exe. [ - Credential Dumping].
This keylogger installs itself as a service and records keystrokes in encrypted files such as thumbcache_96.dbx [ \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information] [3].

They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].

All Rights Reserved 2-1 Overview In an effort to advance the practice of security testing through adversary emulation and adversarial engineering, we present this emulation plan to be used by an adversary emulation team looking to emulate the threat group commonly known as APT3.
The plan includes the group\xe2\x80\x99s commonly known behavior through the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been documented in publicly available threat reporting.
To ground the plan in a common taxonomy, it is based on the MITRE ATT&CK model1.
The scope of this emulation plan covers the adversary lifecycle, beginning with initial network compromise and ending with exfiltration.

Historically, information about attackers\xe2\x80\x99 on-target actions and goals have been difficult to obtain and APT3 reporting is no exception; however, the document bases instructions off publicly accessible sources whenever possible, focusing on sources that could be cross-referenced to some degree.
To fill the intel gaps, the authors relied on their experience in threat intelligence and adversary emulation for best-estimates.
Threat reporting sources vary widely, and correlation of activity to a threat group is not straightforward, and as such the authors have worked to ensure reputable sources are referenced.

While many threat intelligence sources work to provide information that is as accurate as possible to the community, there is still an inherent risk that third-party threat reporting may provide inaccurate information.

For example, they discuss concessions that have been made to make the emulation instructions practical or to indicate where inconsistent or nonexistent reporting has required gaps to be filled in with best-guess estimates of adversary behavior.
References are indicated in-line with bracketed numbers [#] and listed at the end of this document.

It is possible that their strong reliance on credential access (detailed later) allows them to use credentials with increasing levels of access in place of other local privilege escalation mechanisms.
Their perceived focus during this phase, however, is on finding credentials that allow direct admin permissions.
In this case, control falls through to credential access or persistence.
During an engagement, adversary emulators may find it necessary to perform local privilege escalation due to time constraints.
Most common frameworks (including Metasploit and Cobalt Strike) contain some methods for privilege escalation.
Also, UACBypass [24] and PowerUp [9] are common and freely available tools that may be used to perform Privilege Escalation.

Presumably this is done for easier future access.
3.2.1.4 Credential Access APT3 uses many forms of credential access.

They used customized versions of pwdump, and later a custom compiled version of mimikatz, to search for cached Windows credentials [ - Credential Dumping] as well as ChromePass and Lazagne [( - Credentials in Files], to search though browser and other credential caches.

Their pwdump tool injects itself into lsass.exe and is executed by running the GetHash export of the lsremora.dll [3] Mimikatz is used to dump plaintext credentials by injecting into lsass.exe. [ - Credential Dumping].
They also install a keylogger, which can be used to discover credentials and remote systems [ - Input Capture].
This keylogger installs itself as a service and records keystrokes in encrypted files such as thumbcache_96.dbx [ \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information] [3].

This may be due to a lack of available information on how APT3 operates during an operation since most reports tend to be focused on forensic information.
In addition to built-in Windows utilities, there are some open source tools which collect similar information.

APT3 will quickly spread to other machines as fast as possible, often checking for easy password reuse by trying to mount shares from other machines via \xe2\x80\x9cnet use\xe2\x80\x9d [ \xe2\x80\x93 Valid Accounts] [ - Windows Admin Shares] [ \xe2\x80\x93 Brute Force].

Depending on the defensive setup, exfiltration could be much noisier and noticeable than attempting to hide in the noise with lay-of-the-land tools.
The only source we were able to find for APT3 exfiltration methods is from 2012.
For exfiltration, they will identify Office documents on the computer [23] [ - Data from Local System].
They then drop the command-line Chinese language version of WinRAR and use it to compress and encrypt the discovered documents [ - Data Compressed].
This archive will then be stored in the recycle bin [23], usually on a machine designated as a staging server, which they move the exfiltration through [ - Data Staged].
Data is exfiltrated over port 443 which is typically HTTPS traffic, however they have used SSL encryption [17] and normal HTTP [23] [ - Commonly Used Port] .

Once on a machine, the actors collect information about the victim such as connected users [14] and analyze it for its value, trying to determine where they landed and what access they have.

Next they then dump as many credentials as possible, and quickly continue spreading throughout the network.
They specifically go after file servers and print servers [1] [3].

Once they\xe2\x80\x99re moved to all the machines they think have value, they collect all the documents they want, package them up and password protect them, and exfiltrate them out of the organization [15].
In some cases, however, they\xe2\x80\x99ve been known to persist within a network for very lengthy periods without ever exfiltrating data.

3.1 Phase 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Initial Compromise The goal of the Initial Compromise phase is to achieve successful code execution and control of a system within the target environment.
They have used new 0-days on multiple browsers [15].
They have targeted existing 0-days in Internet Explorer [2], Windows [2], and Flash [14].

They have also been known to compromise weakly secured legitimate websites to which users are directed through spear phishing emails [16]. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.
Some of the Pirpi instances have been known to also use SSL for their communications and even include public/private keys within the binaries [17].
This level of C2 customization can be achieved with Cobalt Strike\xe2\x80\x99s malleable C2 profiles, as seen in the accompanying Malleable C2 profile modeled on [14].
3.1.2 Defense Evasion Many of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s open source tools are customized or modified to prevent detection.
These are defense evasion techniques that APT3 sets up before getting initial access to the target environment.
It is recommended to use anti-antivirus (AV) capabilities to prevent AV detection of commonly available tools.
If Sandboxing is a problem, possibly encrypt tools to bypass sandboxing.
An example of this would be Veil-Evasion [18] or Artifact Kit [19].
ATTACK techniques: \xe2\x80\x93 Obfuscated Files or Information, \xe2\x80\x93 Software Packing, \xe2\x80\x93 Indicator Removal from Tools.
3.1.3 Initial Access For Initial Compromise, both web server drive-by and malicious attachments are within APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
The Social Engineering Toolkit (free) [20] and Cobalt Strike (paid) [6] have features that support these methods.
3.1.3.1 Case 1 \xe2\x80\x93 Spear Phishing with Browser Exploit [2] In late November 2014 an APT3 campaign used a spear phishing email (see Appendix A) containing a link to a malicious site.

The second establishes persistence via Schtasks. https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ https://attack.mitre.org/wiki/Technique/ Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited.

Publicly reported direct observation of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s Network Propagation techniques is almost non- existent.
One report that discusses general characteristics of APT3 is [23], but it is uncertain what data sources were used to compile the listed TTPs.
Aside from that report we draw conclusions of how APT3 operates based on the capabilities of Pirpi and other tools that they are reported to use.
There are some persistence techniques that they have used during Initial Compromise that can be applied to Network Propagation.
Despite this, there are significant gaps in the public knowledge of APT3\xe2\x80\x99s tradecraft.
Where necessary we fill in details with best guesses or recommendations.
Each step within this phase is broken out by ATT&CK tactic and the corresponding APT3 specific techniques documented in reports.

All Rights Reserved 3-16 a heavy emphasis on enumerating users in these special groups with the \xe2\x80\x9cnet user\xe2\x80\x9d command [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].

Querying the domain for the \xe2\x80\x9cDomain Admins\xe2\x80\x9d group [ \xe2\x80\x93 Permission Groups Discovery] returns the users that are members of that group, which then involves looking up those users to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re part of any other interesting groups [ \xe2\x80\x93 Account Discovery].

Their perceived focus during this phase, however, is on finding credentials that allow direct admin permissions.
In this case, control falls through to credential access or persistence.
During an engagement, adversary emulators may find it necessary to perform local privilege escalation due to time constraints.
Most common frameworks (including Metasploit and Cobalt Strike) contain some methods for privilege escalation.
